summary: The Comoros-flagged Yara J reported a fire in Romanian territorial waters near Sulina on the evening of 14 October 2026. impact: Romanian Coast Guard statements relayed by both outlets say the crew extinguished the fire and everyone aboard was safe.
evidence: Romania's president, whose country is not a party to the war, said on 15 October that two aerial drones hit the two ships near Sulina, as reported by Spotmedia; he gave no technical details. This conflicts with the defence minister's earlier statement, carried by Digi24, that radar had not shown a drone approaching the ship. Info Sud-Est had cited unnamed sources for a possible drone strike.
unknown: Who launched the drones, how the conflicting official statements are reconciled and the exact strike time are not established. The minister gives a radio alert at 20:23 EEST (UTC+03); ARSVOM gives its rescue request at 20:25. The map marker is a sea centroid, not the ship's position.
attribution: Not established. The president declined to say whether the attack was deliberate or whether Russia was behind it; a shipping-union assertion of an intentional attack is not an official or technical finding.

title: Drones strike cargo ship Chelsea 3 off Byala, Bulgaria; crew of 15 rescued
place: Black Sea, about 18 nautical miles east of Byala (Bulgarian exclusive economic zone)
summary: Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the Maltese-flagged cargo ship Chelsea 3 was hit by three aerial drones about 18 nautical miles east of Byala, in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, during the night of 12 to 13 October 2026. All 15 crew members were rescued.
impact: The Border Police rescued all 15 crew members (seven Ukrainian and eight Azerbaijani nationals) and took them to Varna; five received treatment for minor injuries, according to BTA and BNT, while Sega reports six hurt, mostly with light burns. The ship, sailing empty from Giresun (Türkiye) to Giurgiulești (Moldova), stayed afloat and was at anchor.
evidence: Drone involvement rests on the statement of Bulgaria's prime minister, whose country is not a party to the war, and on the crew, who described three strikes on the deck and side. The national news agency BTA and the public broadcaster BNT report the statement; Sega adds the ship's route and management. A distress signal reached Bulgaria's maritime rescue centre at about 01:30 (Sega: 01:57). Sources give the distance as 15 or 18 nautical miles off Byala.
unknown: Who launched the drones and from where is not established. The exact time of the strike is not given in the cited sources.
attribution: Not established. Radev said there was no solid, clear evidence against any party, while arguing that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation; he said he would summon Russia's ambassador for talks.

title: Cargo ship HS Dignity sinks off Krapets, Bulgaria, after drone attack
place: Black Sea, about 17 nautical miles east of Krapets (Bulgarian exclusive economic zone)
summary: Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said a second merchant ship was hit and sank about 17 nautical miles east of Krapets in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, in the same series of drone attacks in which the Chelsea 3 was struck off Byala on the night of 12 to 13 October 2026. President Iliana Iotova identified the sunken ship as the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship HS Dignity. Early reports had named the Azov Concord; Sega later reported that the Azov Concord had helped in the rescue.
impact: The ship sank. Bulgarian officials said five crew members were rescued and 11 were missing; the prime minister had first reported one crew member rescued. According to Sega, the HS Dignity had a crew of 16 and was sailing without cargo from Algeria to Braila, Romania.
evidence: Reported by Bulgaria's prime minister, whose country is not a party to the war, as one of the ships hit in the night's drone attacks; the ship was identified by President Iliana Iotova. Carried by the national news agency BTA, the public broadcaster BNT, Sega and Al Jazeera. The number of drones that hit this ship is not given.
unknown: Who launched the drones and how many hit the ship were not clear at the time of reporting. Sega places the sinking 17 miles east of Shabla rather than Krapets.
attribution: Not established. Radev said there was no solid, clear evidence against any party, while arguing that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation; he said he would summon Russia's ambassador for talks.

title: Drone strikes tanker Petro Dolphin off Sohar, Oman; two seafarers missing
summary: UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reclassified an incident at Sohar anchorage in Oman as an attack after confirming that a tanker was struck by a drone. India's shipping minister said nine of the 11 Indian crew members were rescued and two remain missing.
impact: India's minister of ports, shipping and waterways said the tanker carried 11 Indian nationals; nine were rescued and two remained missing while the local coast guard searched. A social-media post embedded by The Maritime Executive, citing preliminary information, gives 12 people on board (11 Indian nationals and one Bangladeshi national) with 10 rescued. That is compatible with the minister's figures if the non-Indian crew member was among those rescued, but it is not an official statement. UKMTO said damage and environmental impact were unknown at the time of its update.
evidence: Drone involvement was confirmed by UKMTO, the maritime security reporting centre, which first logged the incident as suspicious activity; 'confirmed' here means confirmed by UKMTO. Both cited articles relay the same UKMTO update and the same Indian ministerial statement, so they are not two independent confirmations. The Maritime Executive dates UKMTO's confirmation to Sunday 11 October; Reuters, via The Jerusalem Post, reported it on Monday 12 October. The Indian government identified the vessel as the Petro Dolphin, a small product tanker.
unknown: Who launched the drone is not established in the cited sources; The Maritime Executive describes it as the latest suspected Iranian strike, without official attribution. The fate of the two missing seafarers and the extent of the damage were not known at the time of reporting.

title: Drones sink cargo ship Alfa Watan and set the Able on fire off Bulgaria; Alfa Watan crew missing
place: Black Sea, about 70 nautical miles east of Byala (Bulgarian exclusive economic zone)
summary: Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said sea and aerial drones hit two Turkish-owned cargo ships about 70 nautical miles off Bulgaria's coast early on 6 October 2026. The Togo-flagged Alfa Watan sank at the scene; the Palau-flagged Able caught fire and its 18 crew members were evacuated.
impact: A Bulgarian ferry and a naval fast boat evacuated all 18 crew members of the Able; two were seriously injured and flown to hospital in Varna. The Alfa Watan sank within minutes. Media reports put its crew at 10 to 12, a number Bulgarian authorities did not confirm; Bulgaria called off the search on 7 October after finding an overturned lifeboat, three life rafts and debris. Early figures from Romania's interior ministry of two deaths and 11 people rescued were not confirmed by Bulgarian officials.
evidence: Drone involvement rests on the statement of Bulgaria's prime minister, whose country is not a party to the war, reported by Al Jazeera with AFP and AP; The Maritime Executive and Novinite report the ships, the rescue and the search. Sources give the distance from the coast as 70 to 80 nautical miles; The Maritime Executive gives the Alfa Watan's registry as Tonga rather than Togo.
unknown: Who launched the drones is not established. The number of crew on the Alfa Watan and their fate were not confirmed, and no drone remains were reported found.
attribution: Not established. Russia's embassy in Bulgaria said the ships were not on the Russian Defence Ministry's target list and called for an investigation. Bulgaria has not assigned blame; President Iliana Yotova called on both Russia and Ukraine to stop attacks on merchant ships.

title: Grain ship Royad Mammadov burns and sinks off Romania; Ukraine blames Russian drones
place: Black Sea, about 20 nautical miles off the Romanian coast (Romanian exclusive economic zone)
summary: The Turkish-owned grain ship Royad Mammadov caught fire and sank in Romania's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea on 5 October 2026; two people were killed and 11 rescued. Ukraine's president said two Russian drones struck the ship; Romanian authorities did not identify a cause.
impact: Two crew members were killed and 11 were rescued by Romanian vessels and helicopters; three injured sailors were airlifted to Constanța. Euronews reported one crew member missing. The ship, flagged in St Kitts and Nevis, had left Izmail in Ukraine's Odesa region bound for Ravenna, Italy, according to Euronews.
evidence: Drone involvement is so far a claim: by Ukraine's president, whose country is a party to the war, and by the head of a Romanian seafarers' union, who said aerial and sea drones were used. Romania's interior ministry reported the fire and the rescue but did not state a cause. Reported by Al Jazeera and Euronews.
unknown: Romanian authorities have not confirmed that drones caused the fire, and who launched them is not independently established. The exact position (Euronews: about 9 nautical miles from the Pescăruș platform, some 20 miles off the coast) and the number of missing crew differ between reports.
attribution: Suspected, not established: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky attributed the attack to two Russian drones; this has not been independently established. The cited sources contain no Russian statement, and Romanian authorities did not name a suspect.

evidence: Two institutional origins are distinguished: the airport operator confirms the restriction, while federal police relay witness reports. unknown: Drone identity, responsible operator and motive are not established. This is separate from the 31 October 2025 BER closure. The municipal point is not a drone position.
attribution: No operator or responsible organisation established by these sources; no criminal charge or conviction is asserted.

title: Authorities report an explosive device attached to a drone in Leipzig/Halle
summary: Saxon investigators reported finding a drone carrying an explosive device overnight on 4–5 August 2026. AP also reported the incident, including a federal minister’s account. This dossier uses the statement date and the expressly reported overnight window.
impact: As of the Saxon investigators’ statement of 5 August at 13:45 local time (CEST, UTC+02:00), flight operations had initially stopped and partially resumed overnight. A separately described unidentified flying object reportedly damaged a freight aircraft; that damage is not attributed here to the recovered drone.
evidence: Saxon investigators are the primary source for the recovered device. AP is a separate newsroom and additionally reports a federal minister’s statement and scene photography, but the device finding rests on the same official investigation, not an independent forensic examination. Later Euronews reporting relays other newspapers’ allegations; it is not a second physical verification.
unknown: The operator, intended target and any connection between the recovered drone and the other unidentified object are unresolved. Later reports concerning a Ukrainian freight aircraft do not independently establish intent or Russian responsibility. Exact flight-suspension times are not provided.
attribution: Not established.

evidence: The sighting rests on reports by two pilots; the closure was described by airport and police spokespeople to AFP. No drone was identified in the cited source.
unknown: Whether a drone was present, its operator and the number of affected flights are not established in the cited source.

title: Reported drones prompt Christmas-period Hannover Airport closure
summary: Reported drone sightings led to a flight suspension at Hannover Airport on 26 December 2025, with disruption continuing into the following day.
impact: The airport operator reports seven diversions and two next-morning cancellations. NDR gives a start shortly before 21:00 and about 3.5 hours; dpa gives 21:47–00:16. The dpa page lead says over four hours, inconsistent with its own detailed times. Exact closure times and duration remain unresolved.

title: Brussels Airport shut twice after drone sightings; Liège airport also suspends flights
summary: On the evening of 4 November 2025 Belgium's air traffic control agency Skeyes halted traffic at Brussels Airport after a drone was seen near the airport. Public broadcaster RTBF reported that Brussels and the nearby Liège airport reopened after an hour and closed again after a second sighting, with normal operations resuming around 23:00. It was the first time Brussels Airport had been shut because of drones.
impact: Brussels Airport said 54 flights were cancelled because of the shutdown, and that about 400 to 500 travellers spent the night there after 41 flights were cancelled and 24 diverted. FlightAware counted 59 cancelled and 43 delayed flights at Brussels on Tuesday. The prime minister convened the National Security Council.

title: Repeated drone sightings over Belgium's Kleine Brogel air base; police investigate
place: Kleine Brogel air base, Peer, Limburg
summary: Drones were reported over the Kleine Brogel air base in north-east Belgium on the nights of 31 October and 1 November 2025. A helicopter and police vehicles pursued the drone on Saturday without success, and a drone jammer could not intercept it. Belgium's defence minister said it was not a simple overflight but a clear command targeting the base, and later described the flights as a spying operation. Police opened an investigation.
impact: No damage or injuries are reported in the cited sources. The sightings prompted an investigation by federal police and military intelligence and a proposed counter-drone package.
evidence: The defence minister said the base's detection system had registered multiple drones, and a federal police helicopter tried to track them. The account of the flights comes from the minister's statements and press reports; police have not released technical assessments of the devices or confirmed launch points.
unknown: The number of drones (reports range from one to three on Saturday evening), their type, who operated them and where they were launched from. No arrests had been announced by 2 November.
attribution: No one has been identified. The defence minister said the flights appeared to be a spying operation aimed at destabilising people and that they involved small and larger drones in two phases; authorities have not publicly attributed responsibility.

title: Oslo Airport closed for hours after reported drone sightings; later reporting says a detection system was down
summary: On the night of 22 September 2025, Oslo Airport closed its airspace after reports of drone observations near Gardermoen. Several flights were diverted and the airspace reopened at about 03:20 on 23 September. A later Dagbladet report says it is still not publicly known whether drones were actually observed, and that a drone detection system at the airport was down at the time.
impact: Norway's airport operator Avinor said the airspace was closed for several hours and several flights were diverted, including one that was rerouted to Copenhagen. The closure came on the same night as the drone-related closure of Copenhagen Airport.
evidence: The closure and diversions are reported by Avinor via NRK and by the European Broadcasting Union's fact-checking desk, which rated that only official statements confirm a drone sighting near Oslo airport. Dagbladet reports that a drone detection system was down when the possible observations were made and that Avinor confirmed this to another outlet, saying it contributed to the closure.
unknown: Whether drones were present at all. Dagbladet reported in October that it is still not publicly known whether drones were observed, and the police district investigating said information about airport systems is classified. Who operated any drones is unknown. Police detained two people that night for unauthorised drone flying in central Oslo; a police attorney said that case appears unrelated to the airport.
attribution: No one has been identified as responsible in the cited sources. Russia has denied involvement in the drone activity that closed the Copenhagen and Oslo airports.

title: Russian drones enter Polish airspace overnight; Poland and NATO allies shoot some down
place: Eastern and central Poland, including the Lublin region
summary: Overnight on 9 to 10 September 2025, drones entered Polish airspace during a Russian wave of strikes on Ukraine. Poland's prime minister told parliament that 19 violations were recorded over seven hours. Polish and Dutch aircraft, supported by other NATO assets, shot down some of the drones. Poland called it an act of aggression and consulted allies under Article 4 of the NATO treaty.
impact: Part of Poland's airspace was closed for several hours and Warsaw's Chopin Airport suspended flights. A house in the village of Wyryki in the Lublin region was damaged and its roof largely torn off; the people inside were not hurt. Drones were found at seven locations, and objects of unknown origin at an eighth.
evidence: Polish authorities recorded the violations and recovered drones at multiple sites, and a NATO spokesman said NATO planes engaged potential threats in allied airspace. Figures differ between sources: 19 violations over seven hours according to the prime minister on 10 September, and 21 drones detected with at least three shot down in the Arms Control Association's later summary.
unknown: Whether the incursion was intentional. Russia's Defense Ministry said it did not target Poland, and Belarus said it tracked drones that lost their course after jamming, while several European leaders said it appeared intentional. The exact number of drones and of those shot down is not settled, and the cause of the damage to the house (drone debris or an interceptor) is described differently.
attribution: Polish authorities and NATO officials treated the drones as Russian, and the Arms Control Association reports that debris analysis by multiple media outlets and Polish authorities indicates Russian origin, likely Gerbera-type drones. A joint statement by the foreign ministers of Poland, Lithuania and Ukraine on 12 September accused Russia of a deliberate and coordinated strike. Russia denied targeting Poland, so responsibility for sending the drones into Polish airspace, and intent, remain disputed; recorded here as suspected.

title: Drone launched from Yemen strikes arrivals hall at Ramon Airport near Eilat; Houthis claim attack
summary: On Sunday 7 September 2025 a drone launched from Yemen struck the arrivals hall at Israel's Ramon Airport near the Red Sea city of Eilat, injuring two people and halting takeoffs and landings for about two hours. The Houthis claimed responsibility. The Israeli military said its systems detected the drone but did not classify it as hostile, so interception and alert systems were not activated.
impact: Takeoffs and landings were halted for around two hours and the airport later reopened for full operations. Israel's ambulance service said a 63-year-old man was injured by shrapnel and a 52-year-old woman was hurt, with Haaretz reporting she was injured after she fell; others received treatment for panic attacks. Airline Arkia said its aircraft were undamaged.
evidence: The Israeli military, the Airports Authority and the national ambulance service all described a drone from Yemen that fell in the arrivals hall area, and the Houthi spokesperson claimed the strike. Israeli Army Radio reported that a preliminary investigation indicated the drone had not been spotted by the air force's detection systems at all, which differs from the military's statement that it was detected but not classified as hostile.
unknown: How the drone evaded classification as a threat, the drone type, and whether other drones in the Houthi operation reached southern Israel; the military said it had intercepted three drones launched from Yemen and did not elaborate on the status of the third.
attribution: The Houthi military spokesperson claimed that a drone directly hit the airport and said airports inside occupied Palestine would be continuously targeted. Israel's military said the drone was launched from Yemen.

title: Drone strikes hit Port Sudan over several days, damaging fuel depots, the airport and the main power substation
summary: From 4 May 2025 drones struck military and civilian sites in Port Sudan, the army-aligned government's wartime base on the Red Sea, over several days. Reported targets include a military base near the airport, fuel depots, the airport, a hotel near the presidential residence and the city's main power substation. Military sources blamed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which did not claim the attacks.
impact: Fuel depots burned, air traffic was halted on 6 May at the only airport still handling international civilian flights, and a strike on the main power substation caused a blackout across the city. The maritime security firm Ambrey reported drone strikes on the container terminal. No immediate reports of casualties were given in the AFP report. Nearly all humanitarian aid into Sudan arrives through Port Sudan, and the UN chief called the reports of attacks a worrying development.
evidence: Officials of the national electricity company and the airport confirmed drone hits, AFP and Reuters correspondents or witnesses reported explosions and smoke, and Ambrey reported drone strikes on the container terminal. Blame for the strikes rests on military sources and residents, not on a claim of responsibility or an independent investigation.
unknown: Who launched the drones and from where, the type of drones, and the full extent of damage and casualties. The RSF's statement did not address the attacks. Sudan's army-aligned government accused the UAE of supplying the drones to the RSF; the UAE has consistently denied backing the RSF.
attribution: Sudanese military sources blamed the RSF, and residents told Al Jazeera they believed RSF drone strikes were responsible. The RSF did not address the attacks in a statement late on 6 May. Sudan's army-aligned government severed diplomatic relations with the UAE over alleged arming of the RSF. None of this has been independently established.

title: Drone strike damages the Chornobyl New Safe Confinement; IAEA later finds it lost its confinement function
place: Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant, Kyiv region
summary: At about 01:50 on 14 February 2025 a drone struck the New Safe Confinement, the structure covering the destroyed Unit 4 reactor at the Chornobyl site, and caused a fire. The IAEA team at the site heard the explosion and saw a breach of the outer layer. In late 2025 the IAEA reported that the strike caused significant structural damage and that the structure had lost its primary safety functions, including confinement, without permanent damage to its load-bearing structures.
impact: No casualties were reported and radiation levels inside and outside the building stayed normal and stable. The IAEA later said the strike did not lead to any release of radioactive material but caused significant structural damage affecting the confinement function and projected lifetime of the structure. Limited temporary repairs were carried out on the roof, and further temporary repairs were planned for 2026 with support from the EBRD.
evidence: The IAEA team at the site heard the explosion, saw smoke, fire and the breach, and was informed by Ukraine that a drone had struck the structure. The IAEA's later statements describe the event as a drone strike, and its comprehensive safety assessment confirmed the loss of confinement capability. The IAEA did not attribute the strike.
unknown: Who launched the drone: AP reported that it was not possible to independently confirm who was behind the strike. The IAEA statements in the cited sources do not state the drone type.
attribution: Ukraine's president said a Russian drone with a high-explosive warhead hit the shell. A Kremlin spokesman denied the claim, saying Russia's military does not strike nuclear facilities. The IAEA did not attribute blame.

title: Drone strikes on Tinzaouaten in northern Mali: rebel coalition says 21 civilians killed, army confirms airstrikes
summary: On 25 August 2024, airstrikes hit the village of Tinzaouatine (Tinzaouaten) in northern Mali near the Algerian border. A coalition of Tuareg-majority groups fighting for independence said drones hit a pharmacy and then people gathering nearby, killing at least 21 civilians including 11 children. Mali's General Staff confirmed airstrikes in the sector and said the precision strikes targeted terrorists.
impact: The rebel coalition's provisional toll was 21 civilians killed, including 11 children and the pharmacy manager, with dozens wounded and enormous material damage. The Associated Press described it as the largest number of civilians killed by drones since the peace agreement between the junta and pro-independence groups broke down in 2023.
evidence: The toll and the description of the targets come from the rebel coalition, a party to the conflict; the army's statement confirms airstrikes but does not address civilian casualties. Neither account is independently verified in the cited reports, and the army statement refers to airstrikes rather than drones.
unknown: The number and identity of the victims, the type of aircraft or drones used, and whether the targets were military. The army describes them as terrorists, while the rebels say civilians were killed.
attribution: Mali's General Staff confirmed airstrikes in the Tinzaouatine sector on the morning of 25 August and said they targeted terrorists. The cited reports do not name who operated the aircraft beyond the army's confirmation, and the rebel coalition's casualty claims remain unverified.

title: Houthi-claimed drone strikes central Tel Aviv, killing one person; Israeli military cites human error
place: Tel Aviv (neighbourhood near the US Embassy)
summary: At around 3:10 a.m. on 19 July 2024 an explosive drone struck central Tel Aviv, killing one person and wounding others in a neighbourhood near the US Embassy. The Houthis in Yemen claimed responsibility. Israel's military said it believed the drone was an upgraded Iranian Samad-3 that had flown from Yemen, and an Israeli military official said it was identified but penetrated Israel because of human error in operating the system.
impact: Israel's emergency services said the body of a 50-year-old man was found in an apartment close to the explosion and four people were taken to hospital with slight shrapnel injuries; AP reported at least 10 wounded, citing local police. The blast blew out windows and damaged cars over a wide area. It was described as the first lethal Houthi attack in Israel.
evidence: Israeli police and emergency services reported the casualties, and the Israeli military described the drone type and its approach from Yemen. The drone type rests on an Israeli military assessment; Israeli media reported that fragments of a drone of a kind widely used by Iranian-backed groups were recovered, and the military had not determined whether it exploded in the air or struck a building.
unknown: Whether the drone exploded in the air or hit a building, the exact number of injured (four slightly wounded in Reuters, at least 10 in AP), and the cause of the failure to sound alarms, which the military is investigating. The Houthis' claim of a new drone capable of bypassing defences was rebuffed by the Israeli military.
attribution: The Houthi spokesperson claimed responsibility on X and said the strike used a new drone called Yafa. Israel's military said it believed the drone arrived from Yemen. Analysts and Western intelligence services have long accused Iran of arming the Houthis, which Tehran denies.

title: Drone attacks hit Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant, including a reactor building, IAEA says
place: Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, Enerhodar area
summary: On 7 April 2024 drones struck the Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, the first direct targeting of the plant since November 2022 according to the IAEA. The IAEA's director general reported at least three direct hits against the main reactor containment structures, and on 9 April another drone detonated on the roof of the plant's training centre outside the site perimeter. Russia and Ukraine blamed each other.
impact: The IAEA said damage at unit 6 did not compromise nuclear safety but was a serious incident with potential to undermine the integrity of the reactor's containment system, and one casualty was reported. Russia's state nuclear agency said three people were wounded. The plant's six reactors had been shut down for months.
evidence: IAEA experts at the plant verified the impact of several drone attacks on 7 April, and on 9 April they heard a loud explosion at the time the plant said a drone detonated on the training centre roof. The IAEA team was denied access to several locations for security reasons. The director general later told the IAEA Board the strike did not compromise nuclear safety in a serious way.
unknown: Who launched the drones and from where: the IAEA did not attribute the attacks. The drone type is not stated in the cited sources. The IAEA could not visit several of the locations where the plant reported attacks.
attribution: Plant officials said Ukrainian military drones carried out the attack, and Russia's IAEA ambassador accused the agency of being afraid to say Ukraine was behind it. Ukraine's UN ambassador called the strike a false flag operation by Russia. The IAEA director general said that whoever is behind the attacks is playing with fire and did not attribute them.

title: Anti-junta forces say 29 drones targeted Naypyidaw military sites; junta says it shot down seven
place: Naypyidaw (military headquarters, Aye Lar air base and Naypyidaw International Airport)
summary: On the morning of 4 April 2024 anti-junta forces attacked the Myanmar capital Naypyidaw with drones in a rare strike on the military regime's stronghold. The shadow National Unity Government said 29 explosive-laden drones targeted the military headquarters and an air base. The junta said its air defences shot down seven drones near the airport and a township and that there was no damage or casualties.
impact: Accounts conflict. The National Unity Government said preliminary reports indicated there were casualties, while the junta said there was no damage or casualties. A source at the airport said it was temporarily closed and a drone carrying a bomb was defused, and a civilian witness quoted by Myanmar Now said the drones landed at the edge of the airport runway.
evidence: The attack is described by both sides: the junta displayed images of downed drones and said it had seized 13, and anti-junta groups published photos of the drones used. Casualty and damage claims come from the parties and are not independently verified; residents near the targeted sites told RFA they were unaware of the attacks.
unknown: How many drones were launched, whether any reached their targets, and whether anyone was hurt. The numbers claimed by the sides (29 launched; seven shot down; 13 seized) cannot be reconciled from the cited sources.
attribution: The shadow National Unity Government and the anti-junta Shar Htoo Waw's Kloud Drone Team, working with units of the People's Defence Force, claimed the attack. The junta did not name who launched the drones in the statements cited.

title: Three US service members killed in one-way drone attack on Tower 22 outpost in northeast Jordan
place: Tower 22 logistics outpost, northeast Jordan near the Syrian border
summary: On 28 January 2024 a one-way attack drone struck a US logistics outpost known as Tower 22 in northeast Jordan, near the Syrian border. US Central Command said three US service members were killed and at least 34 were injured. It was the first attack on US forces in Jordan since the Israel-Hamas war began and the first in the region to kill US troops since then.
impact: CENTCOM said three US service members were killed and at least 34 injured, with eight evacuated from Jordan in stable condition; about 350 US Army and Air Force personnel were deployed at the base. Jordan's government said none of its own troops were hurt.
evidence: CENTCOM described a one-way attack UAS that impacted the base, and Jordan's government spokesperson said the attack was carried out by a drone. Reporting says it is unclear why air defences did not intercept the drone. The outpost is not publicly disclosed by Jordan.
unknown: Which group launched the drone and from where, and why it was not intercepted. The injury figure was expected to fluctuate as personnel received follow-on care.
attribution: The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, a network of Iranian-backed Iraqi militias, claimed credit for the attack, according to Task & Purpose; The War Zone reports the group said it attacked other US bases in Syria and an Israeli naval facility, without naming Tower 22 in the statement it quotes. The US president said the attack was carried out by radical Iran-backed militant groups operating in Syria and Iraq and did not name a specific group.

title: Nigerian military drone strike kills villagers at a religious gathering in Tudun Biri, Kaduna state
place: Tudun Biri village, Igabi area, Kaduna state
summary: A drone strike on the night of Sunday 3 December 2023 hit villagers gathered in Tudun Biri, in Kaduna state's Igabi area, to mark the Prophet Muhammad's birthday. Kaduna's governor said civilians were mistakenly killed by a drone targeting terrorists and bandits, and the army division commander was quoted as saying a routine army mission inadvertently affected community members. The president ordered an investigation.
impact: The National Emergency Management Agency said 85 bodies had been buried while the search continued. Amnesty International's Nigeria office said 120 people were killed, citing its workers and volunteers; VOA reported at least 87 killed and at least 60 injured. Dozens of wounded were evacuated for treatment.
evidence: Kaduna state officials and the army division commander, as quoted in a state ministry statement, described a mistaken drone strike during an army operation. The Nigerian Air Force said it carried out no operations in Kaduna that night and noted it is not the only force operating armed drones. Defence officials later said terrorists had embedded themselves in the village, which the governor criticised.
unknown: The final death toll (85 buried per the emergency agency, at least 87 per later reporting, 120 per Amnesty), the circumstances of the targeting error, and the findings of the presidential investigation. A Nigerian army spokesperson had not responded to requests for comment in the first reports.
attribution: The head of the army division in Kaduna was quoted by the state government as saying the army was on a routine mission against terrorists and inadvertently affected members of the community, and the governor described a drone targeting terrorists and bandits. The air force said it did not operate in Kaduna that night. Amnesty International accused authorities of putting out contradictory explanations.

title: Air strike on Dedebit camp for displaced people in Tigray kills dozens, aid workers say; TPLF calls it a drone attack
place: Dedebit, northwest Tigray, near the Eritrean border
summary: An air strike on a camp for displaced people in Dedebit, in northwest Tigray near the Eritrean border, late on Friday 7 January 2022 killed at least 56 people and wounded 30, according to aid workers and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). The TPLF spokesman called it a drone attack by the federal government. The UN humanitarian office said the attack caused scores of civilian casualties, and aid agencies suspended operations in the area.
impact: Two aid workers told Reuters that at least 56 people were killed and 30 wounded, many of them children, and said the local authorities confirmed the toll. The UN humanitarian office told AFP the attack caused scores of civilian casualties, and it said humanitarian partners suspended activities in northwest Tigray because of the ongoing threat of drone strikes.
evidence: The death toll comes from aid workers who asked not to be named and from the TPLF, a party to the conflict; the UN office's statement confirms civilian casualties but gives no figure. Aid workers described an air raid, and the drone description comes from the TPLF spokesman.
unknown: The exact number of victims, the type of aircraft or weapon used, and the operator. The Ethiopian government, military and prime minister's office had not responded to requests for comment in the first reports.
attribution: The TPLF spokesman blamed the federal government's forces and called it a drone attack. Ethiopian federal authorities did not immediately comment on this strike and have denied targeting civilians during the conflict. The United States condemned the air raid, and the European Union cited the air attack in a statement without naming who carried it out.

title: Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq and Khurais facilities set ablaze in drone and cruise-missile attack; attribution disputed
place: Abqaiq processing facility and Khurais oil field, Saudi Arabia
summary: Early on 14 September 2019, fires broke out at Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq processing plant and the Khurais oil field. Saudi Arabia's interior ministry said both sites were targeted by drones, and the Houthis claimed the attack, saying they used 10 drones. UN sanctions monitors later referred to drones and land-attack cruise missiles being used in the attack.
impact: The Saudi Press Agency, citing the interior ministry, said Aramco's industrial security teams were dealing with fires at both sites, which were later reported under control. Two sources told Reuters that 5 million barrels a day of crude production had been affected, close to half of the kingdom's output. Saudi Arabia said on 3 October that it had fully restored oil output.
evidence: The use of drones rests on the Saudi interior ministry's statement, the Houthi claim and the UN monitors' report, which refers to drones and land-attack cruise missiles used on 14 September. The production figure comes from unnamed sources cited by Reuters rather than an official statement.
unknown: Who launched the attack and from where. The UN monitors said the sites were approached from the north rather than from Yemen in the south and doubted the Houthis' range; the UN Secretary-General reported being unable to corroborate Iranian origin of the weapons. The monitors were not tasked with identifying who was responsible.
attribution: The Houthis claimed responsibility. The United States, European countries and Saudi Arabia accused Iran, which denied involvement. A UN panel of sanctions experts concluded that the Houthi forces did not launch the attacks, and the UN Secretary-General reported that the UN could not independently corroborate that the missiles and drones were of Iranian origin. No attribution has been independently established.
